    19

    22	  - Easy to read generated code as, well, code
    23	  - Can round-trip two different source trees to compare for functional

    25	
    26	- Dump pretty-printing of AST
    27	
    28	  - Harder to read than round-tripped code, but more accurate to figure out what
    29	    is going on.
    30	
    31	  - Easier to read than dump from built-in AST module
    32	
    33	- Non-recursive treewalk
    34	
    35	  - Sometimes you want a recursive treewalk (and astor supports that, starting
    36	    at any node on the tree), but sometimes you don't need to do that.  astor
    37	    doesn't require you to explicitly visit sub-nodes unless you want to:
    38	
    39	  - You can add code that executes before a node's children are visited, and/or
    40	  - You can add code that executes after a node's children are visited, and/or
    41	  - You can add code that executes and keeps the node's children from being
    42	    visited (and optionally visit them yourself via a recursive call)
    43	
    44	  - Write functions to access the tree based on object names and/or attribute names
    45	  - Enjoy easy access to parent node(s) for tree rewriting

    48	    The decompilation back to Python is based on code originally written

    51	    cases when the AST changed on different versions of Python), and its

    24	
    25	``pybv`` is a lightweight exporter to the BrainVision data format. It is meant
    26	for use with electrophysiology datasets stored in the
    27	`Brain Imaging Data Structure <https://bids.neuroimaging.io>`_.
    28

    35	About the BrainVision data format
    36	=================================
    37	
    38	BrainVision is the name of a file format commonly used for storing
    39	electrophysiology data. Originally, it was put forward by the
    40	company `Brain Products <https://www.brainproducts.com>`_, however the
    41	simplicity of the format has allowed for a diversity of tools reading from and
    42	writing to the format.
    43	
    44	The format consists of three separate files:
    45	
    46	1. A text header file (``.vhdr``) containing meta data
    47	2. A text marker file (``.vmrk``) containing information about events in the
    48	   data
    49	3. A binary data file (``.eeg``) containing the voltage values of the EEG
    50	
    51	Both text files are based on the
    52	`Microsoft Windows INI format <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INI_file>`_
    53	consisting of:
    54	
    55	- sections marked as ``[square brackets]``
    56	- comments marked as ``; comment``
    57	- key-value pairs marked as ``key=value``
    58	
    59	A documentation for core BrainVision file format is provided by Brain Products.
    60	You can `view the specification <https://www.brainproducts.com/productdetails.php?id=21&tab=5>`_
    61	as hosted by Brain Products.
    62	
    63	
    64	Installation
    65	============
    66	``pybv``'s only dependency is ``numpy``. However, we currently recommend that
    67	you install MNE-Python for reading BrainVision data. See their instructions
    68	`here <https://www.martinos.org/mne/stable/install_mne_python.html>`_.
    69	
    70	After you have a working installation of MNE-Python (or only ``numpy`` if you
    71	don't want to read data and only write it), you can install ``pybv`` through
    72	the following: ``pip install -U pybv``
    73	
    74	Contributing

    76	The development of ``pybv`` is taking place on

    88	The primary functionality provided by ``pybv`` is the ``write_brainvision``
    89	function. This writes a numpy array of data and provided metadata into a
    90	collection of BrainVision files on disk.

   102	
   103	Currently, pybv recommends using
   104	`MNE-Python <https://martinos.org/mne/stable/index.html>`_

   106	nearly-round-trip conversion of the data (up to the numerical precision you
   107	specify in the ``resolution`` parameter).

   113	    import mne

   116	    raw = mne.io.read_raw_brainvision('tmp/test.vhdr', preload=True)
   117	
   118	    # Read in the event information as MNE annotations
   119	    annot = mne.read_annotations('tmp/test.vmrk')
   120	
   121	    # Add the annotations to our raw object so we can use them with the data
   122	    raw.set_annotations(annot)
   123	
   124	    # Reconstruct the original events from our Raw object
   125	    events, event_ids = mne.events_from_annotations(raw)

def _optimize_channel_unit(resolution, unit=None):
    """Calculate an optimal channel scaling factor and unit."""
    # If unit is explicitly provided, use it
    if unit is not None:
        # Normalize unit representation (support both uV and µV)
        unit_map = {
            'V': ('V', 1.0),
            'mV': ('mV', 1e-3),
            'uV': ('µV', 1e-6),
            'µV': ('µV', 1e-6),
            'nV': ('nV', 1e-9)
        }
        
        if unit not in unit_map:
            raise ValueError(f"Unit '{unit}' not supported. Must be one of: {list(unit_map.keys())}")
            
        display_unit, unit_multiplier = unit_map[unit]
        scaling_factor = resolution / unit_multiplier
        return scaling_factor, display_unit

    exp = np.log10(resolution)
    if exp <= -7:
        return resolution / 1e-9, 'nV'
    elif exp <= -2:
        return resolution / 1e-6, 'µV'
    else:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Test edge cases for the unit parameter implementation."""

import numpy as np
import tempfile
import os
from pybv.io import write_brainvision, _optimize_channel_unit


def test_scaling_correctness():
    """Test that scaling is mathematically correct."""
    print("=== Testing Scaling Correctness ===")
    
    # Test case: resolution = 1e-7 V, want µV unit
    # Expected scaling: 1e-7 V / 1e-6 V/µV = 0.1 µV/V
    resolution = 1e-7
    expected_scaling = resolution / 1e-6  # Convert to µV
    actual_scaling, unit = _optimize_channel_unit(resolution, 'µV')
    
    print(f"Resolution: {resolution:.0e} V")
    print(f"Target unit: µV (1e-6 V/unit)")  
    print(f"Expected scaling: {resolution}/1e-6 = {expected_scaling}")
    print(f"Actual scaling: {actual_scaling}")
    print(f"Unit: {unit}")
    print(f"Scaling correct: {abs(actual_scaling - expected_scaling) < 1e-10}")
    print()


def test_different_resolutions_with_same_unit():
    """Test that different resolutions work with the same unit."""
    print("=== Testing Different Resolutions with µV Unit ===")
    
    resolutions = [1e-9, 1e-7, 1e-5, 1e-3]
    for res in resolutions:
        scaling, unit = _optimize_channel_unit(res, 'µV')
        print(f"Resolution {res:.0e} V -> scaling: {scaling:.3f} {unit}")
    print()


def test_round_trip_consistency():
    """Test that data round-trip works correctly with new unit parameter."""
    print("=== Testing Round-trip Consistency ===")
    
    # Create test data
    np.random.seed(12345)
    data_orig = np.random.randn(2, 100) * 1e-6  # Microvolt-level signals
    ch_names = ['EEG1', 'EEG2']
    sfreq = 500
    
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
        # Write with explicit µV unit
        write_brainvision(
            data=data_orig,
            sfreq=sfreq,
            ch_names=ch_names,
            fname_base='roundtrip_test',
            folder_out=tmpdir,
            resolution=1e-7,
            unit='µV'
        )
        
        # Check header contains µV
        vhdr_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, 'roundtrip_test.vhdr')
        with open(vhdr_path, 'r') as f:
            header_content = f.read()
            if 'µV' in header_content:
                print("✅ Header correctly contains µV unit")
            else:
                print("❌ Header does not contain µV unit")
                print(header_content)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_scaling_correctness()
    test_different_resolutions_with_same_unit()
    test_round_trip_consistency()
